{{Short description|none}}
[[File:Fausto Coppi, Tour de France 1952 01 (cropped).jpg|thumb|alt=A black and white photo of a man in front of a crowd of people|[[Fausto Coppi]], who won the [[Giro d'Italia]] five times between 1940 and 1953]]

The [[Giro d'Italia]] is an annual [[Road bicycle racing|road bicycle race]] held in May. Established in 1909 by newspaper ''[[La Gazzetta dello Sport]]'', the Giro is one of cycling's three "[[Grand Tour (cycling)|Grand Tours]]"; along with the [[Tour de France]] and the [[Vuelta a España]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.uci.ch/templates/UCI/UCI1/layout.asp?MenuId=MTk0Nw&LangId=1 |title=FAQ |publisher=Union Cycliste Internationale |access-date=17 August 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090723024909/http://www.uci.ch/templates/UCI/UCI1/layout.asp?MenuId=MTk0Nw&LangId=1 |archive-date=23 July 2009 }}</ref> The race usually covers approximately 3,500 kilometres (2,200&nbsp;mi), passing through Italy and neighbouring countries such as France.<ref>{{cite news |author=Tim Maloney |url=http://autobus.cyclingnews.com/road/2007/giro07/?id=stages/giro0712 |title=Stage 12 – Thursday, May 24: Scalenghe - Briançon (Francia), 163 km |date=11 May 2007 |work=Cycling News |publisher=Future Publishing Limited |access-date=4 April 2011 |archive-date=8 January 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100108103621/http://autobus.cyclingnews.com/road/2007/giro07/?id=stages%2Fgiro0712 |url-status=live }}</ref> The race is broken into day-long segments, called stages. Individual finishing times for each stage are totalled to determine the overall winner at the end of the race. The course changes every year, but has traditionally finished in [[Milan]].

The rider with the lowest aggregate time at the end of each day is leader of the [[general classification in the Giro d'Italia|general classification]], and since 1931 wears a pink jersey. Other classifications have also been added, and sometimes removed; the leaders of some of these classifications were also indicated with jerseys, whose colours have varied over the years. As of 2011, the Ciclamino(purple) jersey is worn by the leader of the [[points classification in the Giro d'Italia|points classification]]; the Blue jersey is worn by the leader of the [[Mountains classification in the Giro d'Italia|mountains classification]] and the white jersey is worn by the leader of the [[Young rider classification in the Giro d'Italia|young rider classification]].

[[Alfredo Binda]], [[Fausto Coppi]] and [[Eddy Merckx]] have the most Giro victories, each of them having won the competition five times. Coppi is the youngest winner of the Giro; he was 20 years, 158 days old when he won the [[1940 Giro d'Italia]].<ref>{{cite news |url=http://uk.eurosport.yahoo.com/28052010/58/giro-d-italia-top-five-giro-d-italia-finishes.html |title=Top five:Giro d'Italia finishes |publisher=Eurosport |date=24 May 2010 |access-date=4 September 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120614041429/http://uk.eurosport.yahoo.com/28052010/58/giro-d-italia-top-five-giro-d-italia-finishes.html |archive-date=14 June 2012 }}</ref> The oldest winner of the Giro is [[Fiorenzo Magni]], who was 34 years old, 180 days when he won the [[1955 Giro d'Italia]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.procyclingstats.com/race/giro-d-italia/2022/gc/history/youngest-and-oldest-winners |title=Youngest and oldest winners of the Giro d'Italia |publisher=Pro Cycling Stats |access-date=11 September 2022 |archive-date=11 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220911183215/https://www.procyclingstats.com/race/giro-d-italia/2022/gc/history/youngest-and-oldest-winners |url-status=live }}</ref> The fastest victory in the Giro was in [[1983 Giro d'Italia|1983]], when [[Giuseppe Saronni]] won at an average speed of {{convert|38.937|km/h}}.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.dailypeloton.com/displayarticle.asp?pk=5226 |title=87th Giro d'Italia: a bit of History |publisher=Daily Peloton |date=11 September 2003 |access-date=4 September 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100324061338/http://www.dailypeloton.com/displayarticle.asp?pk=5226 |archive-date=2010-03-24 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Italian cyclists have won the most Giros; 41 cyclists have won 68 Giros between them. Belgian cyclists are second with seven victories, and French riders are third with six wins.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.gazzetta.it/Speciali/Giroditalia/2010/en/numeri.shtml |title=Giro's Number |work=La Gazzetta dello Sport |access-date=4 September 2010 |archive-date=29 July 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100729092938/http://www.gazzetta.it/Speciali/Giroditalia/2010/en/numeri.shtml |url-status=live }}</ref> The current champion is [[Jonas Vingegaard]] of [[UCI WorldTeam]] {{UCI team code|TVL}} who won the [[2026 Giro d'Italia]].<ref name=jonas>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cycling/articles/clyp4req9peo |title=Vingegaard seals Giro to add to Tour and Vuelta wins |publisher=BBC Sport |date=31 May 2026 |access-date=31 May 2026 |first=Matt |last=Warwick }}</ref>

==History==
In 1909, the newspaper ''[[La Gazzetta dello Sport]]'' established the [[Giro d'Italia]], inspired by the success of the [[Tour de France]], which started in 1903.<ref>{{harvnb|Foot|2011|pp=13–14}}</ref> The first Giro was won by [[Luigi Ganna]], while [[Carlo Galetti]] won the two following Giros. In [[1912 Giro d'Italia|1912]], there was no individual classification; instead, there was only a team classification, which was won by [[Team Atala]]. The 1912 Giro is the only time the competition has not had an individual classification.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://archiviostorico.gazzetta.it/2001/giugno/09/qual_stato_giro_italia_piu_sw_0_010609313.shtml |title=qual e' stato il giro d' italia piu' lungo, e quale il piu' breve ? |work=La Gazzetta dello Sport |language=it |date=9 June 2001 |access-date=6 September 2010 |first=Giuseppe |last=Castelnovi |archive-date=8 May 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140508223646/http://archiviostorico.gazzetta.it/2001/giugno/09/qual_stato_giro_italia_piu_sw_0_010609313.shtml |url-status=live }}</ref> From 1914 onwards, the scoring format was changed from a points-based system to a time-based system, in which the cyclist who had the lowest aggregate time at the end of the race would win. The Giro was suspended for four years from 1915 to 1918, due to the [[First World War]]. [[Costante Girardengo]] was the winner of the first Giro after the war in [[1919 Giro d'Italia|1919]].<ref>{{cite news |url=http://uk.eurosport.yahoo.com/06052011/58/giro-d-italia-giro-d-italia-numbers.html |title=Giro d'Italia: In numbers |publisher=Eurosport |date=6 May 2011 |access-date=17 July 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110816172848/http://uk.eurosport.yahoo.com/06052011/58/giro-d-italia-giro-d-italia-numbers.html |archive-date=16 August 2011 }}</ref>

[[File:Maglia rosa.jpg|thumb|upright|alt=A pink jersey hung on a coat-hanger, with bikes in the background|The [[General classification in the Giro d'Italia|Pink Jersey]] ({{langx|it|Maglia rosa}}) worn by the leader of the general classification]]
The dominant figure in the 1920s was [[Alfredo Binda]], who won his first Giro in [[1925 Giro d'Italia|1925]] and followed this up with another victory in [[1927 Giro d'Italia|1927]], in which he won 12 of the 15 stages. Victory in [[1929 Giro d'Italia|1929]] came courtesy of eight successive stage wins. At the height of his dominance, Binda was called to the head office of ''La Gazzetta dello Sport'' in 1930; the newspaper accused him of ruining the race and offered him 22,000 [[lira]] to be less dominant, which he refused.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/sport/othersports/cycling/5291484/Giro-dItalia-celebrates-centenary-year.html |title=Giro d'Italia celebrates centenary year |work=The Daily Telegraph |location=London |date=7 May 2009 |access-date=4 September 2010 |first=Brendan |last=Gallagher |archive-date=31 October 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101031095447/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/sport/othersports/cycling/5291484/Giro-dItalia-celebrates-centenary-year.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Binda won five Giros before he was usurped as the dominant cyclist by [[Gino Bartali]]. Nicknamed the "Iron Man of [[Tuscany]]" for his endurance, Bartali won two Giros during the 1930s, in [[1936 Giro d'Italia|1936]] and [[1937 Giro d'Italia|1937]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9A04E3DD1438F935A35756C0A9669C8B63&n=Top/Reference/Times%20Topics/Subjects/D/Deaths%20%28Obituaries%29 |title=Gino Bartali, 85, a Hero in Italy For His Cycling Championships |work=The New York Times |location=New York City |date=6 May 2000 |access-date=5 September 2010 |first=Alessandra |last=Stanley }}</ref> Bartali's dominance was challenged in [[1940 Giro d'Italia|1940]], the last Giro before the [[Second World War]], when he was defeated by his 20-year-old teammate [[Fausto Coppi]].<ref>{{harvnb|Fotheringham|2010|p=37}}</ref>

The rivalry between Bartali and Coppi intensified after the war. Bartali won his last Giro in [[1946 Giro d'Italia|1946]], with Coppi winning his second the following year. Coppi won a further three Giros and in [[1952 Giro d'Italia|1952]] he became the first cyclist to win the Tour de France and Giro in the same year. Swiss [[Hugo Koblet]] became the first non-Italian to win the race in [[1950 Giro d'Italia|1950]].<ref name="cycling">{{cite news |url=http://autobus.cyclingnews.com/road/2009/giro09/?id=/features/2009/giro09_50facts |title=50 Giro facts you need to know |work=Cycling News |publisher=Future Publishing Limited |date=15 May 2009 |access-date=5 September 2010 |first=Greg |last=Henderson |archive-date=13 September 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110913021808/http://autobus.cyclingnews.com/road/2009/giro09/?id=%2Ffeatures%2F2009%2Fgiro09_50facts |url-status=live }}</ref> No one dominated the tour during the 1950s, Coppi, [[Charly Gaul]] and [[Fiorenzo Magni]] each won two Giros during the decade. The 1960s were similar, five-time Tour de France winner [[Jacques Anquetil]] won in [[1960 Giro d'Italia|1960]], and [[1964 Giro d'Italia|1964]],<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/sport/othersports/cycling/picturegalleries/7714900/Giro-dItalia-2010-champions-throughout-the-years-in-pictures.html?image=6 |title=Jacques Anquetil |work=The Daily Telegraph |location=London |access-date=17 July 2011 |date=12 May 2010 |archive-date=6 June 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140606110246/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/sport/othersports/cycling/picturegalleries/7714900/Giro-dItalia-2010-champions-throughout-the-years-in-pictures.html?image=6 |url-status=live }}</ref> while [[Franco Balmamion]] won successive Giros in [[1962 Giro d'Italia|1962]] and [[1963 Giro d'Italia|1963]].<ref>{{harvnb|Sykes|2008|p=35}}</ref>

Belgian [[Eddy Merckx]] was the dominant figure during the 1970s. His first victory came in [[1968 Giro d'Italia|1968]]; another triumph in [[1970 Giro d'Italia|1970]] was followed by three successive victories from [[1972 Giro d'Italia|1972]] to [[1974 Giro d'Italia|1974]], which is the record for the most successive victories in the Giro.<ref>{{harvnb|van Walleghem|1993|p=73}}</ref> [[Felice Gimondi]] was victorious in [[1976 Giro d'Italia|1976]] winning his third Giro. Belgians [[Michel Pollentier]] and [[Johan De Muynck]] won the two subsequent Giros in [[1977 Giro d'Italia|1977]] and [[1978 Giro d'Italia|1978]]. In [[1980 Giro d'Italia|1980]], Frenchman [[Bernard Hinault]], who up to this point had won two Tours de France, became France's first winner since Anquetil in 1964. He would win another two Giros in [[1982 Giro d'Italia|1982]] and [[1985 Giro d'Italia|1985]].<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.cyclesportmag.com/features/grand-tour-doubles-bernard-hinault/ |title=Grand Tour Doubles – Bernard Hinault |work=Cycle Sport |publisher=IPC Media |access-date=17 July 2011 |archive-date=6 November 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111106080324/http://www.cyclesportmag.com/features/grand-tour-doubles-bernard-hinault/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[File:Maurizio-Fondriest-Laurent-Fignon-Giro-1989.jpg|thumb|left|[[Laurent Fignon]] (''right'') in the pink jersey riding alongside [[UCI Road World Championships – Men's road race|World Champion]] [[Maurizio Fondriest]] at the [[1989 Giro d'Italia]].]]
[[Stephen Roche]] was victorious in [[1987 Giro d'Italia|1987]], a year in which he also won the Tour and the [[1987 UCI Road World Championships|UCI Road World Championship]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2007/jul/05/cycling.tourdefrance1 |title=Roche remembers his annus mirabilis |work=The Guardian |location=London |date=5 July 2007 |access-date=5 September 2010 |first=Paul |last=Doyle |archive-date=9 May 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140509021645/http://www.theguardian.com/sport/2007/jul/05/cycling.tourdefrance1 |url-status=live }}</ref> American [[Andrew Hampsten]] became the first non-European winner the [[1988 Giro d'Italia|following year]],<ref name="cycling" /> and [[Laurent Fignon]] was victorious in [[1989 Giro d'Italia|1989]]. Spaniard [[Miguel Indurain]], winner of five Tours, won successive Giros in [[1991 Giro d'Italia|1991]] and [[1992 Giro d'Italia|1992]]. Three-time winner of the [[Vuelta a España]], [[Tony Rominger]] was victorious in [[1995 Giro d'Italia|1995]], defeating the previous winner [[Evgeni Berzin]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/other_sports/cycling/3489619.stm |title=End of a troubled ride |publisher=BBC Sport |date=19 March 2004 |access-date=5 September 2010 |first=Andrew |last=Benson |archive-date=27 August 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070827044742/http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/other_sports/cycling/3489619.stm |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Marco Pantani]] was the winner in [[1998 Giro d'Italia|1998]], a year in which he completed the Tour and Giro double, [[Ivan Gotti]] won the previous Giro in [[1997 Giro d'Italia|1997]] and the subsequent one in [[1999 Giro d'Italia|1999]].

[[Stefano Garzelli]] won the Giro in [[2000 Giro d'Italia|2000]].<ref>{{cite news |url=http://autobus.cyclingnews.com/results/2000/may00/giro00/stages/giro00st20.shtml |title=Stage 20 – June 3: Briancon to Sestrieres, (ITT) 34 km |work=Cycling News |publisher=Future Publishing Limited |date=3 June 2000 |access-date=5 September 2010 |first=Gabriella |last=Ekström |archive-date=28 April 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110428011524/http://autobus.cyclingnews.com/results/2000/may00/giro00/stages/giro00st20.shtml |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Gilberto Simoni]] was the winner in [[2001 Giro d'Italia|2001]] and [[2003 Giro d'Italia|2003]], with [[Paolo Savoldelli]] victorious in [[2002 Giro d'Italia|2002]]. Simoni was denied a third victory in [[2004 Giro d'Italia|2004]], when he was beaten by teammate [[Damiano Cunego]]. Salvodelli won his second Giro in [[2005 Giro d'Italia|2005]], beating Simoni by 28 seconds. [[Ivan Basso]] was the victor in [[2006 Giro d'Italia|2006]], [[Danilo di Luca]] won in [[2007 Giro d'Italia|2007]], though the tour was marred by doping allegations.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/other_sports/cycling/8163587.stm |title=Italian Di Luca fails doping test |publisher=BBC Sport |date=22 July 2009 |access-date=6 September 2010 }}</ref> Spaniard [[Alberto Contador]] of {{UCI team code|AST|2008}} was the winner in [[2008 Giro d'Italia|2008]]; the following year he raced in the Tour de France instead, and [[Denis Menchov]] was the Giro victor.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/other_sports/cycling/8076123.stm |title=Menchov wins Giro despite crash |publisher=BBC Sport |date=31 May 2009 |access-date=6 September 2010 |archive-date=5 June 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090605131807/http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/other_sports/cycling/8076123.stm |url-status=live }}</ref> Basso returned after a doping suspension to regain his title in [[2010 Giro d'Italia|2010]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/other_sports/cycling/8713804.stm |title=Italy's Ivan Basso wins second Giro d'Italia title |publisher=BBC Sport |date=30 May 2010 |access-date=4 September 2010 |archive-date=8 May 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140508222801/http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/other_sports/cycling/8713804.stm |url-status=live }}</ref> Contador was the victor at the podium ceremony in Milan,<ref name="contador2">{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cycling/13589276 |title=Alberto Contador wins 2011 Giro d'Italia |publisher=BBC Sport |date=29 May 2011 |access-date=29 May 2011 }}</ref> but he was later stripped of the title after he was found guilty of doping in the [[2010 Tour de France]]. Runner-up [[Michele Scarponi]] was awarded the victory.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2012/feb/06/alberto-contador-ban-tour-cycling |title=Alberto Contsdor gets two-year ban and stripped of 2010 Tour de France |work=The Guardian |date=6 February 2012 |access-date=6 February 2012 |first=William |last=Fotheringham |archive-date=25 September 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150925131808/http://www.theguardian.com/sport/2012/feb/06/alberto-contador-ban-tour-cycling |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[Ryder Hesjedal]] became the first Canadian to win the Giro in 2012, beating [[Joaquim Rodríguez]] by 16 seconds.<ref name="Hesjadel">{{cite news |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cycling/18229220 |title=Giro d'Italia 2012: Ryder Hesjadel is first Canadian to win the race |publisher=BBC Sport |date=27 May 2012 |access-date=27 May 2012 |archive-date=28 May 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120528042429/http://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/0/cycling/18229220 |url-status=live }}</ref> After gaining the lead after the eighth stage, [[Vincenzo Nibali]] won two more stages to help consolidate his lead and win the [[2013 Giro d'Italia|2013 edition]].<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.cyclingnews.com/races/giro-ditalia-2013/stage-21/ |title=Giro d'Italia: Stage 21 preview |work=Cycling News |publisher=Future Publishing Limited |date=26 May 2013 |access-date=5 September 2010 |first=Daniel |last=Benson |archive-date=2 December 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131202015608/http://www.cyclingnews.com/races/giro-ditalia-2013/stage-21 |url-status=live }}</ref> Colombian [[Nairo Quintana]] became the first rider from South America to win the Giro in [[2014 Giro d'Italia|2014]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cycling/27281510 |title=Giro d'Italia 2014: How Nairo Quintana won his first Grand Tour |publisher=BBC Sport |date=31 May 2014 |access-date=31 May 2015 |archive-date=25 August 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150825123157/http://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/0/cycling/27281510 |url-status=live }}</ref> The following year Contador won the Giro for the second time.<ref name="contador">{{cite news |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cycling/32952922 |title=Giro d'Italia: Alberto Contador wins second title in Milan |publisher=BBC Sport |date=31 May 2015 |access-date=31 May 2015 |archive-date=1 June 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150601214111/http://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/0/cycling/32952922 |url-status=live }}</ref> Nibali won his second Giro in 2016; he finished 52 seconds ahead of second-placed [[Esteban Chaves]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Farrand|first=Stephen|title=Nibali pulls off a Giro d'Italia resurrection - Analysis|url=http://www.cyclingnews.com/features/nibali-pulls-off-a-giro-ditalia-resurrection-analysis/|access-date=28 May 2017|work=[[Cyclingnews.com]]|publisher=[[Immediate Media Company]]|date=29 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161027003050/http://www.cyclingnews.com/features/nibali-pulls-off-a-giro-ditalia-resurrection-analysis/|url-status=live}}</ref> In 2017, [[Tom Dumoulin]] became the first Dutchman to win the Giro, finishing only 31 seconds ahead of Quintana.<ref name="giro-2017">{{cite news|title=Tom Dumoulin wins 100th Giro d'Italia after pulsating time trial finish|url=https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2017/may/28/tom-dumouling-wins-giro-ditalia-time-trial|access-date=28 May 2017|work=[[The Guardian]]|date=28 May 2017|archive-date=23 November Froome]] won the 2018 Giro, becoming the first British rider to win the race. He finished 46 seconds ahead of defending champion Dumoulin, mounting a comeback in the final week which included an  {{convert|80|km|mi}} solo victory on stage 19.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cycling/44277687|title=Chris Froome: Giro d'Italia win's validity should not be questioned|website=bbc.co.uk|date=28 May 2018|access-date=3 October 2019|archive-date=10 June 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200610011750/https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cycling/44277687|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cyclingnews.com/races/giro-ditalia-2018/stage-19/results/|title=Giro d'Italia stage 19: Chris Froome steals maglia rosa with 80km solo attack|work=Cycling News|date=25 May 2018|last=Fletcher|first=Patrick|access-date=3 October 2019|archive-date=5 August 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190805033813/http://www.cyclingnews.com/races/giro-ditalia-2018/stage-19/results/|url-status=live}}</ref> [[Richard Carapaz]] became the first Ecuadorian to win a Grand Tour when he won in 2019.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2019/jun/02/richard-carapaz-cycling-giro-ditalia-grand-tour |title=Richard Carapaz wins Giro d'Italia to make cycling history for Ecuador |work=The Guardian |date=2 June 2019 |access-date=25 October 2019 }}</ref> British rider, [[Tao Geoghegan Hart]], was the winner of the [[2020 Giro d'Italia|2020 Giro]]. He won the race by 39 seconds after entering the final stage of the race, a time trial, level with runner-up, [[Jai Hindley]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2020/oct/25/tao-geoghegan-hart-wins-giro-ditalia-after-coming-through-time-trial |title=GB's Tao Geoghegan Hart sensationally claims Giro d'Italia glory after time trial |work=The Guardian |date=25 October 2020 |access-date=25 October 2020 }}</ref> [[Egan Bernal]] won the [[2021 Giro d'Italia|2021 Giro]], while Hindley won the race a year later to become the first Australian rider to win the Giro.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.cyclingnews.com/races/giro-d-italia-2022/stage-21/results/ |title=Jai Hindley wins 2022 Giro d'Italia |work=Cycling News |date=29 May 2022 |access-date=28 May 2023 |first=Patrick |last=Fletcher |archive-date=28 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230528202250/https://www.cyclingnews.com/races/giro-d-italia-2022/stage-21/results/ |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Primož Roglič]] became the first Slovenian to win the Giro in 2023 when he beat [[Geraint Thomas]] by 14 seconds.<ref name="roglic">{{cite news |date=28 May 2023 |title=Giro d'Italia: Mark Cavendish wins final stage while Primoz Roglic secures first title |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cycling/65741299 |access-date=28 May 2023 |publisher=BBC Sport |archive-date=28 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230528171713/https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cycling/65741299 |url-status=live }}</ref> His compatriot, [[Tadej Pogačar]], won the Giro the following year.<ref name=pogacar>{{Cite web |date=26 May 2024 |title=Giro d'Italia: Tadej Pogacar secures race win on debut as Geraint Thomas finishes third |url=https://www.bbc.com/sport/cycling/articles/c06652p001no |access-date=26 May 2024 |publisher=BBC Sport |language=en-GB |archive-date=26 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240526181452/https://www.bbc.com/sport/cycling/articles/c06652p001no |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Simon Yates (cyclist)|Simon Yates]] won the Giro in 2025, winning the race by 3 minutes and 56 seconds from second-placed rider, [[Isaac del Toro]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cycling/articles/c62v6g9vj7po |title=Giro d'Italia 2025: Simon Yates seals first title as Olav Kooij sprints to victory in final stage in Rome |publisher=BBC Sport |date=1 June 2025 |access-date=2 June 2025 |first=Jack |last=Skelton}}</ref> [[Jonas Vingegaard]] won the [[2026 Giro d'Italia|2026 Giro]], to become the eighth cyclist to win all three Grand Tours.<ref name=jonas />
